course.title: Ship a Per-User Counter on Solana
course.one_line_promise: By the end you can build, test, and deploy a per-user PDA counter program to Solana devnet — even if you've never touched a blockchain.

audience.prior_model: Backend web2: functions, a database, REST handlers. No blockchain.
prerequisites: some TypeScript or Rust exposure helps

terminal_outcomes.statement: build, test, and deploy a per-user PDA counter program to Solana devnet

glossary.def: The unit of state on Solana; programs are stateless and read/write accounts passed to them.
A deterministic address owned by a program, derived from seeds + a canonical bump.

brief.title: Get a program on-chain in ten minutes

objectives.statement: deploy a hello-world program to a local validator and read its log

brief.hook: You've shipped web2 services for years. Today you'll put real code on a public computer that no one — not even you — can quietly change. That shift is the whole game.
brief.concept_spec: What a Solana program is (a stateless, deployed function) and the dev loop: build, deploy, invoke, read logs. Worked example: the default hello-world.
brief.artifact_spec: Build and deploy the hello-world program to a local validator; invoke it; see the greeting in the logs.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: change the logged message and redeploy. Solo: add a second log line. Accept: the new message shows in the validator logs.
brief.the_tradeoff: A local validator is instant and free but throws away state on restart — great for the loop, useless as a record. We move to devnet once the program is real.

footguns: pointing the CLI at the wrong cluster

brief.assessment: deploy hello-world locally and show the changed log line
brief.voice_notes: course opener; spine carries it; the felt 'no one can change it' shift is the hook.

brief.title: Store a number that survives

objectives.statement: explain why programs are stateless and state lives in accounts
write and read a counter held in an account

brief.hook: In web2 you'd just bump a row in a database. Your program has no database — and no memory between calls. So where does the count go?
brief.concept_spec: The account model: programs are stateless; state lives in accounts you pass in. Worked example: an account holding a single u64 count, with initialize and increment.
brief.artifact_spec: A program with initialize (creates the counter account) and increment (adds one), with a test proving the value persists across calls.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: fill in the increment handler (TODO). Solo: add a decrement that can't go below zero. Accept: anchor test shows the count persisting and the floor enforced.
brief.the_tradeoff: Putting state in a separate account is flexible and rent-cheap, BUT you pay rent to keep it alive and must pass the right account in every call — there's no implicit 'this.count'.

footguns: not making the account a signer/payer on init

brief.assessment: anchor test: increment persists across two separate calls
brief.voice_notes: expository backbone; the 'no this.count' line is the aha.

brief.title: Give every user their own counter

objectives.statement: explain why Solana has no mappings and how PDAs replace them
derive a canonical PDA seeded by the user and store per-user state under it

brief.hook: One global counter is a toy. Real apps need one per user. In web2 that's a keyed row; on Solana there are no mappings. So how does each user get their own slot?
brief.concept_spec: PDAs: program-owned addresses derived deterministically from seeds + a canonical bump via find_program_address. Worked example: seed the counter account by the user's pubkey.
brief.artifact_spec: Upgrade the counter so each user gets their own counter PDA, seeded by their pubkey; initialize-if-missing and increment.
brief.exercise_spec: Completion: fill in the seeds array (TODO). Solo: add a second PDA keyed by a string label. Accept: two distinct users get distinct, recoverable counters; a reinit attempt fails.
brief.the_tradeoff: PDAs are deterministic and need no stored key, BUT you must store or recompute the canonical bump, and a sloppy seed scheme is an exploit (collision or spoofing).
brief.assessment: test: two users write and read back their own counter; reinit attempt fails
brief.voice_notes: contested 'why no mappings' — derivation leads (Vitalik craft over spine); cite the grounded rent number once verified.

claims.claim: Solana has no native mapping type; per-user state uses separate (PDA) accounts.
claims.query: Solana account model vs mappings; PDA per-user state
claims.verify: core docs: programs stateless, state in accounts
claims.recheck: solana-dev: Solana_Documentation_Search 'account model state in accounts'

claims.claim: PDAs derive via find_program_address(seeds, program_id) returning an address and a canonical bump.
Rent-exempt minimum for the per-user counter account on devnet, in SOL.
claims.verify: pull live devnet figure; record exact value + date

code_to_ground.what: seeds array for the per-user PDA

open_questions: Show init_if_needed here, or defer the reinit footgun to its own beat?
frozen_facts: Solana has no native mappings; per-user data lives in separate PDA accounts.
Store the canonical bump; recomputing it every call wastes compute and only the canonical bump is safe.

assessment.gate_principle: Completion is gated on a deployed, tested program — never on watching.

proof_matrix.evidence: deployed devnet program id + passing test suite

checkpoints.spec: Explain where state lives and why programs are stateless; name one trade-off.
